cd.name: change directory
cd.summary: Moves you into a different folder. Typing cd by itself takes you back to your home folder.

flags.-P: Go to the real folder that a shortcut (symlink) points to, instead of the shortcut itself.
flags.-L: Follow shortcuts (symlinks) as they are. This is the normal behavior.

shell_notes.bash: In bash 4 or newer, running shopt -s autocd lets you type just a folder's name (without cd) to move into it. The bash that comes with macOS is too old for this.
shell_notes.zsh: If the autocd option is turned on, you can type just a folder's name (without cd) to move into it.

pwd.name: print working directory
pwd.summary: Shows the full path of the folder you are in right now.

flags.-P: Show the real location, with any shortcuts (symlinks) worked out.
flags.-L: Show the path the way you got there, shortcuts included. This is the normal behavior.

ls.name: list
ls.summary: Shows the files and folders in the current folder.

flags.-l: Show the list in long form, with size, date, owner, and permissions.
flags.-a: Also show hidden files (the ones whose names start with a dot).
flags.-A: Show hidden files, but leave out the special . and .. entries.
flags.-h: Show file sizes in easy units like K, M, and G (use it together with -l).
flags.-t: Sort by time changed, newest first.
flags.-r: Reverse the order of the list.
flags.-R: Also list everything inside every sub-folder.
flags.-F: Add a symbol after each name to show its type, like / for folders.

flags.-p: Also create any missing folders along the path, and don't complain if the folder already exists.
flags.-v: Print a message for each folder that gets created.

rmdir.name: remove directory
rmdir.summary: Deletes an empty folder. It refuses to delete a folder that still has something inside it.

flags.-p: Also delete the folders above it in the path, as long as they are empty too.

touch.name: create an empty file
touch.summary: Creates a new, empty file. If the file already exists, it just updates the file's last-changed time.

flags.-c: Don't create the file if it doesn't already exist.
flags.-a: Only update the time the file was last read.
flags.-m: Only update the time the file was last changed.

cp.name: copy
cp.summary: Makes a copy of a file or folder. Write the original first and the place to copy it to second.

flags.-R: Copy a folder and everything inside it. On macOS, a slash at the end of the folder name (photos/) copies only what's inside the folder, not the folder itself.
flags.-r: Copy a folder and everything inside it. On macOS, use -R instead, because -r can behave differently there.
flags.-i: Ask before replacing a file that already exists.
flags.-n: Never replace a file that already exists.
flags.-v: Print the name of each file as it is copied.
flags.-p: Keep the original file's dates and permissions on the copy.

cp.warning: If a file with the same name is already where you are copying to, it gets replaced without asking. Use -i to be asked first.

mv.name: move
mv.summary: Moves a file or folder to a new place. It is also how you rename things.

flags.-i: Ask before replacing a file that already exists.
flags.-n: Never replace a file that already exists.
flags.-v: Print the name of each file as it is moved.

mv.warning: If a file with the new name already exists, it gets replaced without asking. Use -i to be asked first.

rm.name: remove
rm.summary: Deletes files. They do not go to the Trash.

flags.-r: Delete folders and everything inside them.
flags.-R: Same as -r: delete folders and everything inside them.
flags.-f: Force: don't ask before deleting, and don't complain if a file doesn't exist.
flags.-i: Ask 'are you sure?' before deleting each file.
flags.-v: Print the name of each file as it is deleted.

rm.warning: This deletes files permanently. There is no undo.

shell_notes.zsh: zsh asks you to confirm before running rm with * (everything in a folder). bash does not ask.

ln.name: link
ln.summary: Creates a link, which is a shortcut that points to another file or folder. Write the real file first and the new shortcut's name second.

flags.-s: Make a symbolic link, which works like a normal shortcut. Without -s, ln makes a hard link, which is a second name for the same file.
flags.-f: Replace anything that already exists where the link is being made.
flags.-v: Print a message for each link that gets created.

cat.name: concatenate
cat.summary: Prints everything in a file to the screen. It can also join several files together, one after another.

flags.-b: Number only the lines that aren't empty.
flags.-s: Squeeze several blank lines in a row down to one.

less.name: page through a file
less.summary: Shows a file one screen at a time so you can scroll through it. Press space for the next page, / to search, and q to quit.

flags.-S: Don't wrap long lines. Scroll sideways to see the rest instead.
flags.-i: Make searches ignore uppercase and lowercase, unless what you search for has uppercase letters.
flags.-F: Quit right away if the whole file fits on one screen.

head.name: show the start of a file
head.summary: Shows the first 10 lines of a file.

flags.-n: Choose how many lines to show. For example, head -n 5 shows the first 5 lines.
flags.-c: Show a number of bytes (about the same as characters) instead of lines.

tail.name: show the end of a file
tail.summary: Shows the last 10 lines of a file.

flags.-n: Choose how many lines to show. For example, tail -n 20 shows the last 20 lines.
flags.-f: Keep watching the file and show new lines as they get added. Press Ctrl+C to stop.
flags.-F: Like -f, but keeps watching even if the file gets renamed or replaced.
flags.-c: Show a number of bytes (about the same as characters) instead of lines.

wc.name: word count
wc.summary: Counts the lines, words, and bytes (about the same as characters) in a file.

grep.name: search text
grep.summary: Searches for text inside files and shows the lines that match.

flags.-i: Ignore the difference between uppercase and lowercase letters.
flags.-r: Search every file in a folder and all of its sub-folders.
flags.-n: Show the line number of each match.
flags.-v: Show the lines that do NOT match instead.
flags.-l: Only show the names of files that have a match.
flags.-c: Only show how many lines matched.
flags.-w: Only match whole words, so 'cat' won't match 'category'.
flags.-o: Only show the part of the line that matched, not the whole line.
flags.-E: Turn on extra search patterns, like cat|dog to find lines with either word.

find.name: find files
find.summary: Searches a folder and all of its sub-folders for files and folders by name, type, size, or date.

flags.-name: Find things whose name matches a pattern. For example, -name "*.txt" finds all .txt files.
flags.-iname: Like -name, but ignores uppercase and lowercase.
flags.-type: Only find one kind of thing: f for files, d for folders.
flags.-size: Find files by size. For example, -size +10M means bigger than 10 megabytes.
flags.-mtime: Find files by how many days ago they were changed. For example, -mtime -7 means changed in the last 7 days.
flags.-maxdepth: Limit how many levels of sub-folders to search.
flags.-exec: Run another command on each thing that is found.
flags.-delete: Delete everything that is found. Careful: there is no undo.

find.warning: With -delete or -exec, find can delete or change every file it finds. Run it without them first to check what matches.

which.name: find a command's location
which.summary: Shows where the program for a command is stored on your computer.

flags.-a: Show every match, not just the first one.

shell_notes.bash: In bash, which doesn't know about your aliases. Use type instead to see those too.
shell_notes.zsh: In zsh, which also tells you if the name is an alias or a function.

chmod.name: change mode
chmod.summary: Changes who is allowed to read, change, or run a file. For example, chmod +x script.sh lets you run script.sh as a program.

flags.-R: Change the permissions of a folder and everything inside it.
flags.-v: Print a message for each file that gets changed.

chmod.warning: Opening permissions up too far (like chmod 777) lets anyone on the computer change or run the file.

chown.name: change owner
chown.summary: Changes which user owns a file. You usually need sudo to use it.

flags.-R: Change the owner of a folder and everything inside it.
flags.-v: Print a message for each file that gets changed.

chown.warning: Changing the owner of system files can stop programs from working. Double-check the path, especially with -R.

sudo.name: superuser do
sudo.summary: Runs a command as the administrator (root), who is allowed to change anything on the computer. It asks for your password first.

flags.-u: Run the command as a different user you name, instead of the administrator.
flags.--user: Same as -u: run the command as a different user you name.
flags.-g: Run the command as part of a different group (a named set of users) that you name.
flags.--group: Same as -g: run the command as part of a different group you name.
flags.-i: Start an administrator session, so every command you type runs as root until you type exit.
flags.-k: Forget your password right away, so the next sudo asks for it again.
flags.-l: List what you are allowed to run with sudo.

sudo.warning: Commands run with sudo can change or delete anything, including files your computer needs to work. Only use it when you understand the command.

ps.name: process status
ps.summary: Shows programs (processes) that are running, each with a number called a PID that you can use with kill. By itself it only shows the ones started from this terminal window.

flags.-e: Show every process on the computer, including other users' and background ones.
flags.-f: Show more details, like the full command and when it started.
flags.-u: Only show processes that belong to the user you name.

kill.name: stop a program
kill.summary: Stops a running program by its process number (PID). Use ps or top to find the PID.

flags.-9: Force the program to stop immediately, without letting it clean up. Only use this if a normal kill doesn't work.
flags.-KILL: Same as -9: force the program to stop immediately, without letting it clean up.
flags.-15: Politely ask the program to stop, so it can save and clean up first. This is what kill does if you don't give a signal.
flags.-TERM: Same as -15: politely ask the program to stop, so it can save and clean up first.
flags.-HUP: Send a 'hang up' signal. Many background programs reload their settings when they get it, and others just stop.
flags.-l: List the names of all the signals kill can send.
flags.-s: Choose which signal to send by its name. For example, -s TERM politely asks the program to stop.

kill.warning: The program stops and may lose any unsaved work.

top.name: live process monitor
top.summary: Shows a live, updating list of running programs, how hard each one is making the computer work (CPU), and how much memory it uses. Press q to quit.

flags.-o: Sort the list by a column, like CPU use. The column names are different on each system: -o cpu on macOS, -o %CPU on Linux.

echo.name: print text
echo.summary: Prints the text you give it back to the screen. It can also show what a named setting (a variable) holds, like echo $HOME for your home folder.

flags.-n: Don't move to a new line at the end.
flags.-e: Understand special codes like \n (new line) and \t (tab).

shell_notes.zsh: In zsh, echo already understands codes like \n without -e. In bash, you need -e.

clear.name: clear the screen
clear.summary: Wipes the terminal screen so you can start with a clean view. The shortcut Ctrl+L does the same thing.

history.name: command history
history.summary: Shows a numbered list of commands you have typed before. Type ! and a number (like !42) to run one of them again.

flags.-c: (bash only) Clear the whole history list.
flags.-d: (bash only) Delete one entry by its number.

shell_notes.zsh: zsh only shows your most recent commands by default. Type history 1 to see all of them.

man.name: manual
man.summary: Opens the manual page for a command, which explains everything it can do. Scroll with the arrow keys and press q to quit.

flags.-k: Search all the manual pages for a word. Handy when you don't know a command's name.
flags.-f: Show a one-line description of a command.

alias.name: make a shortcut
alias.summary: Creates a short name for a longer command, like alias ll='ls -l'. Typing alias by itself lists all your shortcuts.

shell_notes.bash: Aliases go away when you close the terminal. To keep one, add the line to your ~/.bashrc file (on macOS, ~/.bash_profile).
shell_notes.zsh: Aliases go away when you close the terminal. To keep one, add the line to your ~/.zshrc file.

export.name: share a variable
export.summary: Creates a named setting (a variable) that programs started from this terminal can read, like export EDITOR=nano. It only lasts until you close the terminal.

flags.-p: List all the named settings (variables) that programs can read.
flags.-n: (bash only) Stop sharing a variable with programs, but keep it in this shell.

shell_notes.bash: To keep it after closing the terminal, add the line to your ~/.bashrc file (on macOS, ~/.bash_profile).
shell_notes.zsh: To keep it after closing the terminal, add the line to your ~/.zshrc file.

source.name: run a file's commands
source.summary: Runs the commands from a file inside your current terminal. It is often used to reload your settings after you edit them.

shell_notes.bash: To reload your bash settings, run source ~/.bashrc. Typing a single dot (. ~/.bashrc) does the same thing.
shell_notes.zsh: To reload your zsh settings, run source ~/.zshrc. Typing a single dot (. ~/.zshrc) does the same thing.

exit.name: leave the shell
exit.summary: Closes the shell you are in, which usually closes the terminal window or tab.

shopt.name: shell options
shopt.summary: Turns bash settings on or off, or shows which ones are on.

flags.-p: List every setting and whether it is on or off.

setopt.name: set option
setopt.summary: Turns on a zsh setting that changes how the shell behaves. Typing setopt by itself lists the settings you have changed.

unsetopt.name: unset option
unsetopt.summary: Turns off a zsh setting. It is the opposite of setopt.
